utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, witness. Would you please stand up and make your solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jasarevic. Could you please give your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I am a retired general of the BiH army, and my name is Jusuf Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court, I will lead this witness on his non-contentious background particulars.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, would you just confirm the following information about yourself: You were born in a place called Guvanista in the municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: From 1965 to 1966, you were a student in the military college in Bileca for reserve officers where you were rewarded the rank of reserve infantry second lieutenant. Would you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: A reserve second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right. And in 1979, you graduated from the faculty of political science at the University of Sarajevo. Would you confirm that for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right. And in 1971 you started to work in the Kakanj municipality TO staff as a civilian assistant for operative issues and training. And there you were rewarded the rank of first lieutenant in reserve. Would you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1977, you took a course for assistance of military security in TO staffs. The training was in a military school in Pancevo - I'm sorry about my pronunciation - in Serbia. And this course lasted for three months. Would you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1977, you were transferred to the Municipal TO Staff in Zenica. You were the assistant to the TO staff commander for military security issues. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1979, you were transferred from the Zenica Municipal TO Staff -- sorry, Your Honour. There's no answer to my last question. Would you, Mr. Jasarevic, be so kind as to -- because there's a transcript, we need you to say yes or no quite audibly. So would you confirm the last one. That in 1977 --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If the interpreter would get that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1979, you were transferred to the Zenica Municipal TO Staff to the -- the zonal TO Staff in Zenica. You were the assistant for military security in that TO Staff. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In November 1984, you became deputy assistant for morale in the republican staff TO. You were the deputy for information and propaganda but you held this position for a very short time, three to four months. Would you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: After this stint, you were transferred to the Intelligence Department to the position of assistant to the chief of the intelligence department in the BiH republican TO staff. You were still a civilian serviceman in military terms and your position was equal to that of major or lieutenant colonel. Would you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At the end of 1984 until 1986 while the TO was evolving, intelligence and reconnaissance, you had two more training courses again in Pancevo . Each course lasted for about one month.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On 1st November 1988, you were transferred to the Sarajevo District Staff TO where you became the chief of military security department in that TO staff.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You then became the chief of military security of the District TO Staff and your headquarters were in Ciglani where the joint command of the army of the Federation of BH is now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In December 1991, you were awarded the rank of lieutenant colonel in reserve.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You worked in this military security of the Sarajevo District TO Staff until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On 15th April 1992, a new TO was formed, and this TO was renamed the TO Regional Staff, and you worked there until the end of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At the beginning of August 1992, you came to the Main Staff. The chief of the Main Staff was then Sefer Halilovic. The Main Staff was in the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So until February 1993, you became the chief of the counter-intelligence section of the military security department and at the same time you were Kerim Lucarevic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Lucarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Thank you for pronouncing that to me. At the same time, you were appointed to the position of chief of military security of the Supreme Command Staff and you became the deputy of Fikret Muslimovic. Would you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I was the chief of department or section for counter-intelligence in the administration for security, which was headed from February 1993 by Mr. Fikret Muslimovic, and in that capacity I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. On July 7th -- on about the 17th of July, you were appointed to the position of chief of military security of the Supreme Command Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your current occupation is chief of regional department for de-mining in Sarajevo of the Ministry for Civil Work, and you're a retired brigadier general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but now it is not chief but head. However, the position has remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I would like to now show you MFI202, Your Honour. That will be the new number. And it's 00554725.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we refer to Sanction, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- that that be identified by reference to the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I will be giving the witness a B/C/S version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you look at that, Mr. Jasarevic, and tell us where did your particular department, the military security, fit in in the overall military and political structure of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It is in this part which is marked by Roman numeral VII, where it says "the administration for security."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And under who were you? Can you tell us under which entity you were under, your military security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: My security administration that I headed was all the time linked with the main commander of the armed forces. Up to the month of June, the chief of Main Staff occupied that position. And when as the function of the commander developed, my superior commander was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute. I think Your Honours are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just intervene briefly. I'm not going to object to this document at all, but the accused man hasn't got a copy. Because we're using Sanction -- this problem was raised in the past. And what I'd ask is that the accused, Mr. Halilovic, be given a copy of this document in B/C/S so that he can follow what's being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think that's a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, all of this has been disclosed, and this is the same concern that Mr. Morrissey expressed last time, and I'm going to say the same thing. All of these documents have been disclosed to them in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But now we are using the e-court system. The Defence is expecting the B/C/S appear on the screen. But when we are using Sanction, I think, you know, we have some disadvantage by providing the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you bear with me for a minute, the case manager has got a wizard solution to this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Our case manager -- sorry, Your Honour, our case manager informs me that what she can do is put it both onto the screen. It may not be as big, but nevertheless she can put the B/C/S version on the screen for the benefit of the accused. Would that be agreeable, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could try that as a practical solution. I just want to ensure that it's big enough for Mr. Halilovic to see. But let's try it and we'll see. Might Ms. Delalic approach, please, to relay what Mr. Halilovic can see and can't see back to counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Just the last word on that, Your Honours. Since the counsel have always been given a list of the exhibits in advance and they do have the B/C/S, they should be able to print it out in future or, if they want, they could ask me and I could print out an extra copy for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If -- may I then put it on the record I do now ask that it be printed out each time that Sanction is being used, because we don't have Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Always happy to oblige the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Now, under what law and regulations did the military security operate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The military security was regulated by the decree law that was adopted by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 1992. Pursuant to this law and based on the law on the national security which was adopted by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this regulation was adopted in February 1992. We drafted a book of rules for the work of security in the armed forces, and this was done in the -- on the 11th September 1992. This book of rules provides for the organisation and tasks of the military security services in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were these based on any other rules of any other army? This -- did you adopt this from any other army?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Part of these solutions were mostly adopted to -- adapted to the former JNA, and they were then adapted to the conditions that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina found itself in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go back to this document. I believe everybody now has it on -- on the screen. And could you tell me: Can you explain this, please. How many -- you have at the top a commander; right? At the top of this chain.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how many deputy commanders are there? If you look at the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: There were two deputy commanders of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Staff until the man in the position of commander was introduced. At that moment, the Chief of Staff became the deputy commander. So for a while we have a situation in which three deputy commanders co-existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was your chain of authority, the military security? By this, who did you answer to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The chief of military security administration was answerable to the commander; before him, to the Chief of Staff. Exceptionally, if the commander was absent, it was the deputy commander who took his role, and in that case I was reporting to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would it be any one of these three deputy commanders? In the -- in the event that a commander was not available.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It would be the Chief of Staff, because he was more involved in all the other activities. However, since during this period of time the situation was what it was, I was never in a position to have to answer directly to the Chief of Staff or any of his deputies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did your administration, security administration, have a command function?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who gave you orders which you had to obey?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It was the commander. It could be the president of the state, the president of the Presidency, but that happened rarely or better say never. It was done through the commander or the first person in the command chain of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So who was the military security subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did President Izetbegovic give you any direct orders? Did he have the ability to give you orders which you had to obey?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No. He did not give me any tasks directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did he have the ability to if he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. He was the president of state. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you would get your orders from the commander of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, who could you give orders to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I could give orders to members of the security administration that consisted of some 30 men. And as for the other tasks, I would send them in the form of instructions, as a professional guidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And did you have to inform anyone of the -- of the activities? The security administration officer, would he have to advise anyone in their field of activity? Who would they keep informed on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military security service was in charge of state security in the armed forces. It was part of the command staffs and institutions of the armed forces. It is immediately subordinate to the commander. And whatever information it obtained through its professional work, it was duty-bound, and this was done as much as it could be done -- it was duty-bound to inform its superiors. In more specific terms, we provided our information in two forms: One was the form of a bulletin on a daily basis, and special information if we had some particular task. We submitted those regularly to the commander, to the president of the Presidency, to the Ministry of Defence, to the Prime Minister of the government, to the Minister of the Interior, and for the most part to Mr. Ejup Ganic. I'm not sure why we sent these to Ejup Ganic, in the light of the fact that he did not have any specific position, unlike the ones that I mentioned previously. However, he was a very important member of the Presidency, and he very often stood in for the president and he wanted him to have this information. Whatever the security services obtained in the form of information, they didn't keep for themselves but they forwarded this information to the five or six places that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you yourself, before you forwarded this information, would get it from the military security officer subordinated to various units, corps, battalions; is that right? I'll come in a minute about the structure.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The principle based on which the security services worked was the same as that applied in command. You didn't skip any levels. What I'm trying to say is we obtained information in principle from the security service of the corps and indirectly from the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the -- the military intelligence department, was this a separate department?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how these two services were organised in our army. In a certain way this was something that was copied from the former JNA; namely, the intelligence service gathered intelligence on the enemy. The counter-intelligence service, which is how we referred to it, which was to all practical intents the military intelligence service, was mostly into counter-intelligence as regarded its own armed forces. The work of the military security service of the armed forces was organised based on three functions: The first and primary function was counter-intelligence; the second function was staff security; and the third function was the military police. So it was these three functions that the service was in charge of according to the book of rules, and these were the tasks they had to perform to the extent that they were able to under the prevailing circumstances, wartime circumstances, the drawing-up of reports that I've mentioned and forwarding these reports to their superiors. Vital issues were relayed in special reports and not in orders or in expert instructions, as we called them, according to the rules of service. Underneath there were the brigade security services. In the brigades, you had the battalion-level security services. So in actual fact, we have four levels of organisation in our security service. It is important to point out, Your Honours, that on all of these different levels the security service was subordinated exclusively to the commander as concerned control and command. Within the service, there was the possibility of professional guidance, but this did not empower anyone to give orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you said there were four levels. Can you please tell the Court what these four levels are, starting from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The first was the security administration. This was a body attached to the staff of the Supreme Command or the staff of the Main Staff, the Supreme Staff, as it was called later. It had a number of departments or sections. One was for counter-intelligence, and this was the strongest section -- or rather, department, which had five subsections. It had a section for staff security and a section for the military police. All the while, there were -- there was a section for legal affairs and analysis sector. There was a lawyer who worked throughout the war in the security administration, and he was the best qualified person to review information from a legal point of view. As for the analysis section, this section was in charge of processing such information as was obtained, and then based on any such information, drawing up reports to be sent to the superior positions that I've mentioned. This is how the administration worked. This administration had between 30 and 40 persons working there. We were never fully staffed. We were always short of staff. Corps level, there were different --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now you're talking about -- if you can just name them. This is level 2, corps level.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's the next level from the top down, the corps level. At this level, there were security departments which in principle comprised all these functions that I referred to while talking about the previous one. These departments had 15, 16, or 17 staff, depending. Professionally subordinate to them, on the third level were security services of the brigades. These were sections comprising six or seven persons. Their departments were not as evolved as those at corps level, but in principle they, too, carried out the three functions that I mentioned: Counter-intelligence, staff security, and military police. The fourth level of the security services was that of the battalions. In terms of number of executors, this was the lowest level. They had an assistant commander for security-related affairs, and there's an interesting detail in relation to this. At this level, the function of security and intelligence was merged. This officer usually had an assistant, so there were usually two of them. If there was an independent battalion, this required three persons to do the job. Your Honours, I deem it important to point out that at all these various levels there was a military police presence, except at battalion level. I'm not sure about the presence of military police in any independent battalions, but as a matter of principle the military police were not present at battalion level. If I may be allowed to say something about the strength of the military police at all these various levels. At brigade level, there was a military police platoon comprising about 30 persons. When I say a platoon, that means 30 men. At corps level, there was a military police battalion, which as a matter of principle contained three companies, between 200 and 300 strong, depending on the needs. And there was a unit attached to the platoon comprising between 10 and 15 men who were specially trained for analysis and inspection. These were professional persons working within the military police who had a certain level of authority. At the level of the Main Staff, there was a military police battalion. At the beginning, they had some difficulties setting up this battalion as a qualified competent military police unit. This was because throughout 1992 and early 1993 there -- there were difficulties in Sarajevo in getting people organised and setting up the military police. As early as in 1992, the military police battalion that was established did not really work properly. It went on like that until maybe April or May 1993 I emphasise, Your Honours, that all these military police units, wherever they existed as I pointed out, were exclusively under the jurisdiction, under the command of the commander of the unit which they formed part of. At the level of the Main Staff, they were under the command of the Chief of the Main Staff, later the Commander, at the corps level, under the command of the corps commander, at the brigade level under the command of the brigade commander. Only the person who held that position – the commander - could issue orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what about operating groups and tactical groups?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Those were provisional formations. They did not have a permanent structure, in terms of organisation and establishment, unlike the units that I have so far been talking about. These formations would be organised whenever necessary in order to carry out certain tasks in certain areas. By setting up an operations or tactical group -- an order to set up one of these would indicate how it should be organised and what structure it should have, indicating also the strength of the members of military security to be included. So this was a provisional structure, or these were provisional formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Jasarevic, I'd like to show you a document, and that is MFI203, number 02131159.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We'll refer to Sanction, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can I please be told what 65 ter number that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may remind counsel, that this is actually a Defence document. It's -- which they agreed that I may use. It's the rules of service on military security.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, was this the document under which and these are the rules under which the military administration operated?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the rules under which the military administration operated in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the last page of this book of rules, you will see that it was adopted on the 11th of September, 1992 by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and signed by the state president, Alija Izetbegovic, personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if I could take you to Chapter 6, paragraphs 45 and 46. If you could please have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Chapter 6 speaks about the competencies and the work of the security administration. Please can you give me the paragraphs again?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, 45 and 46. Basically all of them, but -- but if you could just sort of tell us when you said that they're all under a commander - and that would be 46 - would that be the correct position? 46. If you'd look at 46. What it says there: "Security administration shall be headed by a commander who shall be responsible to the commander of the Main Staff of the armed forces for the organisation of work and a legal, correct execution of assignments within the competency of the security administration or Minister of Defence on questions pertaining to the role of jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence for security of the armed forces of the republic. "

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, which leaves nothing unclear. Chapter 6 talks about the security administration, and items 8 and 9 from the same book of rules, paragraph 8 and 9, talk about the overall structure of the service. Paragraph 46 speaks about the fact that the security administration is in charge of the -- of professional guidance and organising tasks from its own purview of activity, and this regulation too was created for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. So Chapter 2 is the tasks of the military security service. Could you look at those, please. You just told the Court about the various tasks, and tap ter 2, section 5, it talks about the various tasks. And there are six tasks listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said Chapter 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Chapter 2, yes, the tasks of the military security service. It's on my page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness has still got in front of him in the B/C/S version parts 45 and 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: He actually has a -- a printed ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly Mr. Halilovic would have in front of him parts 45 and 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm finished with 45 and 46. Now I'm looking at Chapter 2, "The tasks of the military security service." Page 4 in the B/C/S. Number 5. If the witness can perhaps refer to Sanction himself. I can't for the life of me understand what's happened to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Can I continue now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, please do. Look at number 2, section 5. And then you have (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f), which are six specific tasks. Can you perhaps sum up for us what the essential aspects of these tasks are, in your own terms, as to what you saw your responsibilities as.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: A while ago, when I spoke about three primary fundamental functions of the military security service, I spoke about the task under Chapter 5, "Tasks of the military security service." This implies a peculiar kind of activity because these activities are usually carried out in secrecy by the enemy, in terms of how they are organised. And that is why the military security service in -- in jargon internally is usually referred to as the secret service, because the methods of work that it applies in its work are those usually applied by the secret services. Under (c), we see: "Procure, update, systemise, and verify data concerning members of the aggressor formations and citizens who aided and abetted the aggressor," from their own ranks is the implication. Under (d): "Detect, monitor documents, and create conditions for intercepting terrorist activity planned and carried out against one's own armed forces." Under (e): "Detect, monitor, and prevent activity by individuals, groups, and organisations whose activities take the form of sabotage, subversion against one's own units." And under (f), I think the protection of intelligence. This refers to reports on combat activities and other important actions.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The specific feature of command in the military security is the fact that it has dual command. And when I say "dual," I mean that control and command implies the unity of command in any military structure and there's no two ways about it. What we mean by "dual" is when we talk about the professional guidance in the military security bodies at all levels, and this specific nature is the result of the fact that part of the security is also counter-intelligence. The military security service would often obtain information that were just -- that was just indications that had to be verified from various sources using various sources, and whenever possible they had -- that information had to be corroborated by documents in order to give them the quality as required by the command and control function. If this had not been done, they could have been misconstrued, and that is why the military security service had to have a professional influence going down the ladder. What do I mean by that? The security administration had influence on the security of the corps. The security corps had the influence on the security of the brigade. And the security of the brigade had influence on the security of the battalion. When temporary groups are formed, that is, operations group and tactical groups, then special orders are issued in order to deal with the issue of this relationship. What one has to bear in mind is the fact that everything started and finished with the commander of the unit at which the security as a service was developed, and this is when it comes to the function of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What about seniority within this? Would a security assigned to a corps be more senior than a security assigned to a brigade and to a battalion and so on and so forth? The seniority amongst the security, those assigned to corps and those assigned to brigades and battalions.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that I've already explained that. Yes, in professional terms, in terms of professional guidance, that is. For example, this is the professional part. This has nothing to do with order-issuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the first function, which is counter-intelligence, this part was the most prominent obligation within the vertical functioning, and that is for the information to be forwarded to the highest possible level where there was enough professional expertise to analyse and verify this information, and if it was at all possible, this information was sent from the very bottom to the very top. When it comes to the staff security function where the situation was assessed at the level of the command, where the service was assigned, where there was training, where -- this remained at the same level. There was no need whatsoever to -- to go up the ladder to the very top; although, even in this part the superior bodies of the security services did have an influence on their superiors, demanding them to maintain a certain level of quality whenever that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, you said one of the tasks --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Now I would like to take you to another aspect of your duty. And can you tell me: Who was responsible for investigating crimes committed by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this particular task of the military security.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Under Chapter 2, "Tasks of the service," 5(b) talks about the counter-intelligence tasks within the service in order to document war crimes that were committed as part of the aggression. What I notice here in the third line from the top down, it says: "Particularly with regard to identification of individuals, groups, and aggressor units which carried out preparations," and so on and so forth. The provision here obviously assumes that war crimes were committed against our own structures by the aggressor. I do believe, however, that this can also apply -- can also apply to cases where members of our units have committed a crime. At the beginning of paragraph (b), it says that: "Conditions must be created for the fullest possible documentation," which means that all steps are taken to create the relevant documents, this being one of the crucial tasks of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And when these security officers detected some of this activity, who would they report it to, which is envisioned in (b), 5(b). Who would they inform?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: They must inform their own commander, their first superior. They must. Since we are talking about activities from Chapter 5, "Counter-intelligence," this sort of information should also be forwarded to the superior security service. If this information is obtained, if such actions are committed, if information is obtained by the security service of the brigade, they would inform the brigade commander and then up the chain of command, also their superior, at corps level.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. I'd like to now come to another topic altogether with you, and I would like to ask you: Who would be responsible for investigating crimes committed by the military personnel within the various levels of corps, brigade, battalions, et cetera? I'll be coming into more detail into this a little later, this particular other tasking.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It would always be the unit commanders. They are the authority responsible within their own units, and the same applies to this. Professionally speaking, military security bodies and military police bodies would also be responsible. Chapter 40 of the book of rules in front of us says that: "If there is a suspicion that a crime has been committed, the security service should take appropriate steps." Chapter 41 says that: "At brigade level or a higher level of authority, their own services should prosecute any such cases as may have occurred."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can we look at Chapter 40 now, which -- can you read 40 and 41 and tell us in your own words what exactly that means. Let's look at 40 first.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I've just said about paragraph 40, when a reasonable suspicion exists that a criminal offence has been committed, that must be prosecuted by military courts, and war crimes would fall under this definition. Officers of the military security service are the ones who are responsible for taking necessary measures to find the perpetrator, to prevent the perpetrator or his accomplice from going into hiding or escaping, to uncover and protect any evidence, and to gather any information useful for the prosecution of this crime." And then paragraph 41 proceeds to explain about the respective levels. I'm sure that the author of this document bore in mind the fact that at brigade level there was a body comprising five or six persons who can deal with the job at battalion level and press charges eventually, charges brought before a military prosecutor, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And did the commander of these units have to approve any investigations which were initiated by the military security detail?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. As I've already said, the commander holds a position of authority. He's someone who would approve a proposal like this coming from a military police body. If no such proposal arrives for a variety of different reasons - they had no knowledge, no will, or no ability, for example - then there was no approval. So if there is no approval and a commander is aware of an act like this having been perpetrated, it's his duty to order -- to issue the appropriate orders. By this definition, the commander is responsible for everything that happens within his unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what if the military police had initiated some investigations? Would they have to inform the military security and the commander?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, they would. But this would not stop them from taking certain steps once having found out about the crime. They'd start collecting evidence and intelligence, but they could not launch an investigation, a full-scale investigation, before consulting with the military prosecutor. We had an investigative military judge at the time. I think this position no longer exists. The incumbents had to be authorised members of the security service or the military police. Not just any police officer would have qualified for that position. Only those who had proper authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, would the security officer have to alert the commander about a crime which had been committed by military personnel? And in what format would this happen?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As long as he knew, yes. But the security officer could not take certain kinds of steps in the brigade, such as, for example, carry out investigations, summon witnesses, have interviews, and gather intelligence. If there were on-site investigations or inspections to be carried out, that would have constituted a serious case of meddling with the control and command system. A commander must know about these things, because these steps might interfere with other activities. Under certain conditions, the commander must approval this or even order this, if no such orders were issued by these lower-level organs to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, how was this information relayed to the commander? Was it in writing? Was it orally?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: This always depended on the objective circumstances. If the objective conditions allowed, this would be done in writing or by communications equipment, which means orally or through direct contact. Bearing in mind the sort of thing that happened during the war in our area, it was very difficult and only rarely that this was done in writing for the brigade to address their commander in writing about any of these steps. In fact, I don't know of a single case like that. Usually it was done orally, in direct contact, or through communications equipment, if no physical contact was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, in the event the commander did nothing with this information, what would the military security officer do next?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with cases like that. But if we speak about a war crime, for example, which falls under paragraph 5 that I have referred to, there is a line of communication leading to the superior security organ, and this kind of information would eventually reach this officer. Any security officer who was in possession of this sort of information, not having been allowed by the commander to do anything about it, would have been duty-bound to report to his superior security organ. Again, the example of brigade and corps levels. The brigade-level officer would have to inform the corps-level officer if at all possible, practicable.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then it would continue going up that chain.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this -- this was always the principle that had to be applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, who actually supervised these investigations?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Once an investigation is under way, the only qualified body that could be in charge is the military prosecutor. The military prosecutor would file requests asking the military police and the security organs at the appropriate level to send him additional information, clarifications, any case material that might be relevant for taking appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So how many ways were there to initiate an investigation? Can you just tell us each way this could be done, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question. I'm not sure if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you can tell us which ways were they within the -- the -- the army to initiate a particular criminal investigation. You've said one is that the military security officer, the police. If you can give us the -- the various ways how an investigation would be initiated. How would it come about? A crime has been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It is essential for a crime to be reported, for people to know that a crime occurred. Whoever received word of this in any of the military structures would have been duty-bound pursuant to the general rules to inform their superior. If they were in no position to inform a security officer, it would have sufficed for them to inform their superior. This applied to private as well as to high-ranking officers. When word was received of something like this, there had to be a -- a lightning-quick reaction. The best thing would be if this information reached the security organ at the respective command, the military police, or the commander in person. These are the three levels, the three institutions in a manner of speaking, that knew what steps were then to be taken. The essential thing, if at all possible, was to identify the vital issues as soon as possible, issues that may be of relevance to a future investigation, which means, if possible identifying the perpetrator, the crime itself, the time, and any evidence. This is what usually constitutes an inspection, which leads to charges being pressed. It's not important who takes these steps. The important thing is that these steps are taken, that no shroud of silence falls over the act so that the crime is eventually forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then the military prosecutor's office, what would that -- what would their role be? Would that -- was that another way?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as my familiarity with the law goes, there was a possibility for the military prosecutor - I'm not sure if I should say "duty" - as soon as a military prosecutor in any way finds out about a crime like that, must react quickly and send a request to one of the military institutions or bodies. Usually the body addressed would be the military police. The prosecutor should request that information be forwarded on the crime. That's how communication between the military police and the military prosecutor usually came about, that is, a body of military security, on the one hand, and military security, on the other. Both of these were duty-bound to comply with the military prosecutor's request.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And would he ask other agencies to assist him in these investigations, the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably, especially we speak about the Ministry of the Interior and their bodies present in the area, professionally qualified bodies. In our circumstances in the first two years of war and even later, we trained our security bodies and our military police all the time. We had to do things in our stride and we had to train people in our stride to perform certain tasks. But our internal affairs bodies were well qualified to come to grips with these tasks. The military service could also, of course, request -- request information from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was the powers of the commander in respect of initiation and terminating investigations?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: A commander is always the person responsible for anything that happens in his own unit. He had the authority, the power, to order an investigation to be carried out by his own bodies, military security bodies or military police bodies. By doing that, he exercised a right that was within his power. Being what he was, a commander, he would later be informed about the course of the investigation but he would no longer deal with the nuts and bolts of the matter. He would appoint other bodies to -- to deal with these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could he terminate any investigations which had been started by either the security service or the military police?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, not. There were, unfortunately, cases. I can't think of any specific ones in terms of where they occurred or who was involved, but there were cases, especially at the lower levels, without sufficient military experience, where commanders failed to identify their own duties and instead prioritised certain combat assignments, which means that they failed to identify the crime as quickly as the situation required; although, this was no general rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So therefore what's your view on the matter as to whose primary responsibility was it to control his subordinates and to react if there was information about crimes committed by these subordinates?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: In terms of orders, the commander would bear this responsibility. Professionally speaking, the security service and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What -- what in the event the commander did not have military police to assist him? What -- what would he -- could he do then?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He could ask his superior to borrow in a manner of speaking a military police unit from the adjacent, neighbouring unit in order to have this task carried out. If there was an order or a directive, depending on the level on which a certain activity was carried out, saying that commanders of the same level had a duty to coordinate on these matters, then the situation could be dealt with swiftly and in a direct manner, not through his superior. But this was not so often the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So a commander, in other words, could request other units and other corps to assist him in any matter concerning his own corps or area of responsibility or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure if this applied to all issues across the board, but when speaking about the military police what I told you is certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was the system of keeping records on the activities of the security services? How did you keep your records? Was there any standard format?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for the operative part that I talked about at the beginning, under item 5 of the Rules of Service, this was done with register books and the sort of information entered would be intelligence issues, counter-intelligence, and other sensitive issues. These files could not be inspected by anyone save for the security bodies. As for all other issues at corps level, the security service would be in charge of a counter-intelligence plan. Everything else that falls under paragraphs 2 and 3 would be done on a monthly basis and take the form of plans and drafts for command activity. This was part of work planning in every command and in every staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And these reports would go up to the military security of the Supreme Command Staff eventually?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As we said, there are four different military security levels. The counter-intelligence level went up the chain of command. If a security counter-intelligence organ in the battalion was in possession of a piece of information that they failed to forward to the corps or the administration but, rather, only sent it to their own superior, in professional terms the brigade, this would complete the extent of their duty. The brigade-level man would assess the information and either deal with it immediately at the battalion brigade level or, if it was a more complex matter, it would be forwarded to the corps security. So much about that level. All other information from the police area and military security area would form part of the so-called regular reports that were submitted to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what kind of training were these -- these security officers given to do their job?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Very early on we realised that the -- the education and training levels of our members and especially specialists - and this includes military security services and the military police - we realised that this was a problem and this was something that we had to deal with. In practical situations, we encountered that problem quite a lot, especially in Sarajevo in 1992, as I have already said, and in 1993. We had a problem. All members of the army wanted to be military policemen because they, I suppose, thought that they would have more authority. They didn't know what that was. And as much as this was possible, we tried to organise and implement certain training schemes. Obviously those training courses were very short, very basic. We didn't have the time to organise more extensive, better organised seminars and courses. And the same was true of the security organs. As a country, as a state, we were being created during the war and we did not have well-trained people who would work in the security. A lot of people in the security did not want to work in the security. It is a very responsible -- a very demanding job which called for certain professional skills, starting with the -- being abreast of the regulations, being a moral person, being able to apply certain methods of work, especially in -- within the counter-intelligence. Counter-intelligence is a profession that calls for a very high level of professionalism. In 1992, I organised in the then-Hotel Belgrade a training course for certain officers of the military police who had already shown certain elements of non-military behaviour, which at the time I couldn't qualify as a particular breach of discipline. I had to explain to them what the military police was, what their tasks would be. I told them that the military police should not be so numerous. It was a very painstaking job. As we grew as the army and as we created certain conditions, we organised training at various levels, at the corps level. Later on in Zenica a school was organised - the name was Ros - the war officer's school. This was where education could be planned and organised in a better way than at the beginning. We cooperated with the -- the organs of the interior, especially in terms of the education of the authorised members of the military police that I've already mentioned. Several officers underwent such courses, at the Ministry of the Interior with some results. Not enough, not as much as we needed. But all this time there was a continuity of education to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What about investigation techniques? Would you use any other agencies to teach them that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Whatever I have said so far, and particularly what was organised in the MUP, had to do with investigation. To be more specific, from the military police battalion, from the General Staff, several people were sent to those courses in order to learn about the investigative techniques. However, we lacked equipment for investigation. We didn't have a camera. We did not have the equipment to fix evidence, not even -- let alone to the investigation of a more complex criminal case such as murder. We had to refer cases to the MUP because we did not have our own means and our own personnel who would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was any training given on the international humanitarian law, law of warfare, protection of civilians, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Our military and state leadership very early on issued certain regulations and directives. I can't quote them because I can't remember them. However, they did channel those activities. I can say that all the courses and seminars contained those things. Allow me to say that at all levels of command a lot of warning has been -- had been given and it was insisted that the international humanitarian law should be observed to the extent we knew and could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasarevic, before I ask you about these particular sections that we've had now before our screen, was there a difference between military discipline procedures in peacetime and in wartime?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Especially when it comes to the urgency of reaction, the speed of reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And I believe Article 19 talks about the conduct of proceedings in -- in peacetime. You have the document before you, Mr. Jasarevic. And the time limit for instituting and conducting proceedings is -- is 30 days in peacetime. And now when we come to the sections 67, 68, 69, that would be accountability in a state of war. Now, can you tell us what the difference is in respect of that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me just repeat what I said a little while ago. The issue of military discipline is within the authority of other organs of the command as well, and it is not primarily one of the tasks of the military security services. Obviously the military security services will also monitor the -- the discipline situation because at the end of the day it may fall under the scope of the interests of the military security services when military discipline breaches start containing elements of crime. All the organs, and especially the organs for morale, guidance in the army, dealt with these issues. Later on military disciplinary courts were organised, and they were the ones that assessed the military discipline. I can only point out in this case that dealing with disciplinary issues from the simplest to the most complex ones in the times of war, which is also corroborated by the articles that we have mentioned, that is, 67, 68, and 69. In 69, the time period of 24 hours is mentioned. In other words, it was important to deal with disciplinary issues very urgently, and this is the specific nature when we compare this situation with the times of peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you look at Article 74, please. Would you tell us according to that article who shall supervise the implementation of these particular rules.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Here it says that: "The chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces" -- and if you'll allow me to draw a parallel with the Article 66 of the rules on the military security, the Article 76 of rules for the work of the military police, this is the first person in the army. When these documents were passed, this was the Chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces. And later on when the function of the commander was developed, it was the commander, and this is implied in the interpretation of these functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could you tell me: When you wrote your -- your report, who would you send them to? Who were your addressees?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I could send my reports in two aspects: One would be the results of the operative counter-intelligence work, and this kind of report would be sent to the five or six addressees that I mentioned earlier on. All the other reports were within the sphere of command and control of the unit to which the service was assigned, and these reports would be sent to operative organs. For example, the operative centre existed at the level of the General Staff, and it was -- this was the organ that collected all the operative reports from the subordinate units and from the units at the level of that command and based on these reports, they would draft a summary report that would then be sent to the commander at that particular level where this particular summary report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, who would appoint military security officers? How were they allocated? Who appointed them to the various levels?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Military security officers were appointed by commanders; however, the organs of the security services played a very important role in the selection process. At the beginning of the war, these officers, security officers, were created so to speak at the will of the commanders of many units, especially the units at the level of battalions and brigades. Later on we succeeded in the majority of the units to secure the principle according to which the military security services did have an impact on the selection of these officers. However, in all of these units -- in many of these units, we for a long time we were not successful at that. To answer your question, it was the commanders who appointed these officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Jasarevic, can you tell me that -- I'm sorry, I'll go back again with my question. You were in July of 1993 the chief of the counter-intelligence section, you informed the Court earlier on. Did you hear of any crimes committed by the ABiH army at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, I was an officer within the administration. I did not receive all the information from the corps level, and so on and so forth. However, I did receive information and I was aware of some cases. I had heard the details of these cases. That's why I knew that there were such breaches of discipline that could constitute crimes. In one case, a possibility was mentioned that a crime had been committed in the area of responsibility of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now go to the time when you've been appointed as the chief of the military security department. Can you tell us: At that time, what did you hear about any crimes committed by any units? Can you tell me about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't provide you with many details; however, it was a known fact that in some units, especially in the units of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, there was a lack of discipline, particularly in the 9th Motorised Brigade and in the 10th Mountain Brigade. On this occasion, I would like to point out as follows, Your Honours: Usually in our jargon we say that it was the 10th and the 9th Brigades. However, to be very precise, one has to say that only a small number of members of these brigades committed those crimes. Each of these brigades had five to 6.000 people. They defended a very large part of the town of Sarajevo. And most of the members of these brigades were honest people. A very small number of people were involved in the breaches of discipline, and at that time we were dealing with the problem of this lack of discipline, which escalated gradually and contained elements of serious crimes, especially when we came by indicia that war crimes were committed in the area of responsibility of that particular brigade, of the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in July 1993 in respect of these two brigades. Did something happen?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The 9th Brigade -- and again, when I -- when I'm talking about brigades, bear in mind that I am referring to just one small number of their members. Members of the 9th Brigade were involved in an incident. They committed a breach of discipline by having attacked the operative centre of the General Staff in the town of Sarajevo. This was a very serious incident. All the officers considered this a serious incident; however, there were no serious consequences. This happened at the beginning of July. I -- at the time, I was not the chief of security, and this incident happened during the night between the 2nd and the 3rd of July, 1993.
