I might be misunderstanding what's in the heading "Comments made by witness during proofing," but it looks very much to me has if this witness has told the Prosecutor already in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know. I know that. But we have to put this in the record, so we -- we'll allow the Prosecution to ask some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I abide by Your Honour's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The reason I'm putting this document to the witness is because he says although he's not seen it before, he knows this information and in fact used this very information to write his own reports. And that is the reason I'm showing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, can you tell us what kind of a document this is, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: At the time this document was produced, I was not chief of the security administration. I have never seen this document before, but I realise that it talks about a breach of discipline by Mr. Ramiz Delalic. That's the only thing I can tell you about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And if you look at the -- the substance of this document, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this procedure. Now, the -- the document has now entered into the record, and the fact is the witness has been crystal clear about his status. And I don't understand the need to proceed this way, but it's not within the procedures of this Tribunal or any court that I'm aware of to -- to proceed any further. Now that the witness has said he didn't see it, Your Honours, it's a -- there's an appropriate way for the Prosecutor to elicit this evidence, and that's to ask the witness what he knows. He can -- that's admissible. It's relevant. It may possibly help this Tribunal to determine certain matters, such as the notice that Mr. Halilovic had, might have had, or could have had. But to put this document now when he says explicitly that he hasn't looked at it is just leading because it's leading in the sense that he's -- it's putting information before the witness and asking him to comment, which is just another form of a leading question. If the Prosecutor was to say to -- was to put a proposition to this witness and say, "I put the proposition that Mr. Delalic did A, B, and C, and D, do you agree," then there would be an objection as to leading. By doing what the Prosecutor is now doing, my learned friend is doing precisely that, putting an answer before the witness and asking him to comment. There's no objection Mr. Jasarevic is an experienced officer and doubtless he can comment on what he saw and what he knew. But this procedure now is, in my submission, once it's stripped back to its essentials, is leading because he says he's never seen this document and it's not his. So for that reason, it shouldn't be persisted with and that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana, I think the witness said it very clear that he's never seen this document and this is the only thing he could tell us about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness is quite clear he's not seen the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But he knows about the incident. And I'm talking about this particular incident, Your Honour, which is reflected in the information. And I wanted to put the information and ask the witness is this the information that he himself was told, although not the document itself. Your Honour, this is -- we have to proceed in this manner, Your Honour, because there are many other documents, and I understand my learned counsel's -- Defence counsel's objections because there are going to be other documents in the same strain. And this was allowed by Your Honours when we took the witness Gusic. And these are documents. It is his area. He's talking about this very incident. And during proofing he actually did say, Your Honour, that he can confirm the information, because that was the very information he did have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could ask some questions about the incidents that happened there. Then after that we'll see if there's any necessity to refer to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, could you tell us about this particular incident of the -- the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've been very clear about it. This document was produced on the 2nd of June. At the time, I was in no position to be aware of this sort of information. Given my position at the time, I heard that Ramiz Delalic, the person referred to in this document, had committed certain breaches of discipline. As for the description of his actions here, this is something that I was not familiar with in great detail at the time, in view of my position at the time as a counter-intelligence officer. Whereas, what's happening here in this document would fall under the second or third area that we talked about earlier. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid this is all I can say about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know what led to this particular incident, this taking -- attacking the police station?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is the public security station in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, forwarded to the intelligence service of Sarajevo. This is the town centre at the period under consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the question, Mr. Jasarevic, was: What led to the 9th and 10th Brigade laying siege on that particular security station?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection to Mr. Jasarevic answering from his own knowledge, but I don't know that he needs to have that document before him anymore. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm going to show the witness another document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Well, if there's another document, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, we have some problem with the e-court system, so the document is not available on our screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I heard it's coming, but it's time for a break. Could we take a break first?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have 30 minutes' break. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I was going to show the witness on our 65 ter list, it's 161, 04035834, and that would be MFI205. Your Honour, before counsel rises to his feet, it is another one of these documents with the -- where the witness had not seen it before, but I would nevertheless show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, there is an objection. There's -- even though it was said before I rose to my feet, I still rose to my feet. Your Honours, because the objection -- Your Honour permitted my learned friend to ask some preliminary questions of the last -- on the last occasion. But you can see from item 161 that it's not necessary for those questions to be asked, because if you look in the right-hand column, Mr. Jasarevic has indicated very clearly what his position is: "I do not know this document." Now, to show him the document, therefore, is just an impermissible leading question and a waste of time. If there's an incident about which my friend wishes to ask, then surely the issue is ask both that incident. If it's relevant to the Prosecution case, there can be no objection to it. But it's really relevance. At the moment showing him a document about something which he knows nothing about is irrelevant, leading, and offends on all sorts of bases, so I do rise and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite understandable, but we should have that answer in the transcript, you know. So still I'll allow Ms. Chana to ask some preliminary questions on this document as well as the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would say before I show the document to this witness, Your Honour, I will refer Your Honours to your own practice directions on the admissibility of evidence. Your Honour, the other thing is the function of us cutting down on our witness list quite dramatically whereupon we have to show documents and this witness has already said he knows the information and it has been done before, and there is barring any -- any objection on authenticity and genuineness of the document, Your Honour, I would still maintain our position that the witness may -- I may refer the witness to the contents of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you could have a try, but -- but we'll see, you know, what's the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What's the answer of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasarevic, do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'll give the B/C/S version to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where is this document from? Who's the author?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the preliminary question has got to be asked first: Has he seen this document before apart from the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, have you seen this document before other than at the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember having seen this document before. The Prosecutor asked who the author was. It's the public security station of Stari Grad. More specifically, Mr. Enes Bezdrop [phoen], whom I know, but I have never seen this document before nor do I remember what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you look at the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think at that point, I submit that there's just no point asking this witness about that document any further. An incident can be asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I agree with you that -- maybe you could ask about that incident directly without referring to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On 2nd July 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the document be returned to the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since the witness has already had this document at his hands, maybe we could proceed

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, as -- it's -- the witness has to be, in my submission, advised that he's being asked to deal with his own memory and not from that document, and of course in those circumstances he doesn't need to refer to the document. And I've got no objection to him referring to his memory at all. He should. But the utility of having the document sitting there in front of him, in my submission, is negligible or zero. And although it may not confuse the witness, it may. Because if he's got a document there, he may think or believe he's being asked to comment on it. And so I submit that once the document has been proved to be absolutely unrelated to him, then there is no need for it to sit there. And it's not an insult in the witness in any way. In fact, I'm sure that he would deal with it in perfect good faith. But there's just no utility in it, so therefore I ask that it just simply be returned to the Prosecutor, where it came from, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you just not look at the document as you reply to my questions, please, Mr. Jasarevic, in this respect. On 2nd July, 1993, what happened and what do you know about it and was this information passed around?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, between the 2nd and the 3rd July some of the members of the 9th Motorised Brigade attacked in a manner of speaking the operations centre of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had an opportunity to discuss this with people who were there at the time, such as, for example, General Zicro Suljevic, General Rifat Bilajac, and so on and so forth. This was an attack, an unusual act perpetrated by some of the members of the 9th Brigade. I am not familiar with any details, such as how long it lasted, but I know that the incident did not result in any injuries to the officials of the centre. In view of my position at the time as a counter-intelligence officer, I really have no further details on that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you don't know what it was that led to this particular attack?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well, I will now show you another document, which is -- 65 ter is 159. It's 04036215, and it's MFI206.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can I have the Bosnian version given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, could you please tell us where does this come from and who is it to.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have seen this document before. This is a proposal being made to me, addressing me by my name, and it was written by the chief of the military security service at the time. By looking at the handwriting and signature, I recognise that this was in the hands of General Fikret Muslimovic. The top left-hand side, where it says "Ivica," that's my own handwriting. I received this proposal or this task from the person who was my superior at the time, and I tasked an operations officer from my own department, Ivica Pinjuh. That was the gentleman's name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What does --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: With checking, in accordance with this proposal, what needed to be checked and to act accordingly, to take a statement from this source of information. Now, what happened later in connection with this particular assignment is not something that I can remember at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what does the figure "0023" mean? At the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we had to protect ourselves in a way, those of us who worked in the field of military security, especially with operative assignments. In order to protect ourselves, we used these codes and marks. I can't remember now whose name this was or who the code was in reference to, which operations officer, but the code stands for an operative signature. That means you knew exactly at the time who produced this official note and forwarded it to the chief of administration, General Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you look at the first paragraph of this document, please. And can you tell us in your own words what that is about.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The text says: "Operative" -- "Operational source." I've spoken a great deal about operative work today -- this is an operational source who provided the operations officer with this information. It is stated here that there has been new information related to Ramiz Delalic. Further, it says that on the 4th of July, around 2200 hours, he turned up at the 9th Brigade police base, his own brigade, therefore accompanied by his assault company and so on and so forth, saying what is stated here: “I have been to Sefer's. He said the Laste would attack us tonight." 16 The Laste, or swallows, is a police unit, an MUP unit. Delalic then told the combatants to take positions around the kindergarten in Svetozar Markovic Street and be ready to strike back. This is obviously a rumour, but it was not to be underestimated, and Your Honours, we were not in a position to 20 verify what the source had said. However, given what was at stake, we had to react as fast as possible, and that's why this operations officer, Ivica Pinjuh was tasked with this. And I think it is very likely that the code number that we can see here is in reference to this operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And now, let's look at the second paragraph of this document. Can you tell us what -- what's said there.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see that the source of this information, on the 3rd of July, Saturday, at Dom Ljiljana, the army centre. According to the source, Ismet Bajramovic, nicknamed Celo, brought the munition from Musan Topalovic, nicknamed Caco, the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade who had taken up positions at the Djuro Djakovic cinema and on top of the Upija building, on the roof. This is a spot in the centre of town between the army centre and the Presidency headquarters, which at the time was also the Supreme Command headquarters. Nearby is the Upija building. There's nothing I can ascertain about this document that it doesn't already state in no uncertain terms. I never verified this information following this proposal. It was taken to have come from a serious source and the operations officer was sent back to the source to elaborate on this, which is a form of monitoring and verifying whether something would actually happen or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'll take you now to the third paragraph, and I will read it to you and then I'll ask you a question. It says: "I will contact the operational source in relation to taking a statement regarding the above-mentioned problems because I find that Sefer Halilovic's direct command over the coup can be documented from these claims as well as the involvement of Ismet Bajramovic, aka Celo, who was impartial and elitist [indiscernible] and in the BiH army." Now, can you tell me what do they mean when they use these words "over the coup"? What's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That is how an operations officer saw the problem or, rather, his source. In relation to the incident between the 2nd and 3rd of July, the so-called attack against the operations centre of the army, whether someone actually used the term "coup," I wouldn't be inclined as a serious person and a serious officer to describe that incident as a coup, which is a very grave thing indeed. It was wartime, and this is what the situation was. I never disregarded or ignored any bit of information, and I would not have been inclined to disregard this either; however, describing it as a coup, I think that's something that we have to chalk down to that particular operations officer and I don't think I would agree with this qualification.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, which incident would they be referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: We can see that here the operations officer links this form of behaviour as described in paragraphs 2 and 3 in reference to Mr. Delalic and Mr. Bajramovic to what is described in the last paragraph, namely, Mr. Sefer Halilovic. And probably, although I can't be certain, if he referred to a coup, he was probably referring to the incident that occurred between the 2nd and 3rd. But as I said, I can certainly offer no guarantees about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this incident which occurred on the 2nd and the 3rd, which incident would that be, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about when members of the 9th Motorised Brigade attacked in a manner of speaking - I'm using the word "conditionally" here because it doesn't tally with my military definition of the term - anyway, they attacked the operations staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I will now show you another document, if I may. And that is -- the 65 ter is 169, 04036166, is MFI207.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have already cleared this with the Defence. This is our exhibit list, but the -- the B/C/S version that we had in the Office of the Prosecutor was one without this particular witness's notations, personal notations on the document. But we -- we found that the Defence document, the same document, has indeed got the -- the witness's personal notations, and the Defence have no objection for me to show them the Defence translation of this particular document. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I take that back. That is in respect to the next document, the -- the Defence -- whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, can I just confirm what it is that we have on the screen. Is it the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's the -- the one I've just read out. The 65 ter is 169.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this document, Mr. Jasarevic? Who is it from? Who is it to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document was in my hands. The handwritten part in the upper right-hand corner is my handwriting. I did that while I was the chief of the security administration. The signature is by Jozo Jozic, who was then the under-secretary of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina in charge of the State Security Services, and it points to the fact that -- that the police station in Hadzici had been attacked on the 8th of September during the night. He indicates in this document that the unit whose officer was Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was involved. When I received documents from various institutions, from the Ministry of the Interior, from the State Security Services most often, or when I received documents from the security services of the corps, I took all of these documents seriously because they arrived from serious institutions. I could not ignore such documents. I could not keep them to myself. That's why I tasked the section for analysis, which was an integral part of the administration that I headed at the time, to carry out two tasks: One of them was to summarise this information and publish it in the Bulletin. The Bulletin was the publication that was published by the administration for security almost every day and delivered it to the five or six institutions or persons that I have already mentioned. The second task I gave to this section was to write a letter to the military security services of the 1st Corps asking them to issue a criminal report, and this would serve for the military police of the 1st Corps to collect additional information in addition to the initial one. And this was how it was done, I believe. Although I can't remember all the details as I sit here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This Bulletin, who did it go to? Who were the addressees that you said you gave this task about [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The Bulletin was sent regularly together with special information to the commander, Mr. Rasim Delic, to the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, to the Minister of Defence, to the Prime Minister in the government, and to the Ministry of the Interior as well. Although sometimes the information that we received came from his people, from his bodies. However, this showed our position and -- towards the information that we received from them. And as I've already said, we often sent this information to Mr. Ejup Ganic, a member of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this information -- and if you look at the body of the document -- was about an armed attack on 8 September at 0430 hours at a checkpoint near Pazaric. It says here: "Armed attacks were carried out by units of Ramiz Delalic, aka Celo, in which Delalic also took part. The attack was proceeded by the regular halt of the vehicle in which Mr. Delalic and his fellow passengers were" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that goes any further, I'm sorry, we don't have the English version of this at this stage. The document that we had on our screen was very much briefer than that. It was a one-paragraph document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. This is only page 1. Maybe you could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I believe we have it now. Would Your Honours excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should indicate to the Court, and I -- I'm -- there's been no objection to this document up to this point. But as I understood the position, this evidence is admissible because it goes to evidence that Mr. Jasarevic is giving concerning matters within his knowledge, within his domain. Ultimately, of course, this is all relevant to one thing only, and that's the notice of Mr. Halilovic. It could never be led as evidence of what actually is supposed to have happened at Pazaric. So I call on the Prosecutor to make it quite clear what the reason for leading this evidence is, bearing in mind that Your Honours refused to entertain the admission of this evidence when it was tried by two other counsel on the Prosecution team through members of the 9th Brigade on different occasions to prove that such an incident took place, a new rule that that was irrelevant. Now, it may be relevant because this witness has put some instructions on it. And that's why I haven't objected thus far. But if it's being led as to the truth of the contents, well, it's at least triple hearsay right now, and I'm going to object to it on that basis. Perhaps my learned friend could say what the relevance of showing this document is right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance is absolutely obvious. The time frame is 8 September. It's about the units. It's about where they were at any particular time. It's about their conduct. And all of this is directly relevant to our charges. And therefore I really cannot see the Defence objection, Your Honour, in respect of the relevance and the units involved, which is Celo's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, so that my friend can see it and so it's quite clear, Your Honour will recall the objection I made last time perhaps. There is no issue as to timing. It's all been agreed blissfully between the parties that these units set off on the 7th. And Your Honour put me to the question when I -- when this was raised last time as to timing. Mr. Re, who appeared at the time, said, "Your Honour, this matter goes only to one thing, and that's timing." And I made the concession in court that well, we -- we concede that timing and there's no issue between the parties about it. But this couldn't be admitted in a tribunal of law as to the truth of its contents. It's third-hand or fourth-hand material. It can be admitted in -- on the basis that I -- as I understood this other material is being led, to show perhaps that it was that some incidents were known about and perhaps people should have drawn conclusions from those incidents, if they knew, if my friend is actually prepared to ask that question. But it's not admissible on the basis my friend seeks to lead it, so since she's indicated it, I object to it being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, I think I made myself very clear that we'll deal with the admission of this document at a later stage. At the same time, I'll allow the Prosecution to use this document -- I mean, to show it to the witnesses to see what we could get from this witness. And later on we'll decide whether this document is relevant to this case or not. That's another matter. So, Ms. Chana, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I was just reading to you the content of this particular information that you said you passed to -- to all these individuals that you listed earlier on, which is the highest-ranking command and political leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And -- and I was reading through it, and it says how he -- "Delalic" - and I'll carry on reading - "refused to show identification to the members of the police while insulting them with offensive words and firing a couple of shots in the air above the heads of the policemen Ejub Hadzic and Enes Sabic. When the police confronted Delalic, around 50 members of his units arrived in to the site in two trucks from Igman Mountain. Celo's soldiers then disarmed policemen and were shouting and swearing after which they physically attacked Hidajet Selimovic, Enes Sabic and Ejub Hadzic and beat them up with rifle butts. As a result of serious injuries, the head, the body, and the dislocation of the hand, Hadzic was transported to the hospital near Tarcin," et cetera, et cetera. Now, this was indeed the information that you passed on to your superiors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It is. And also to the security services of the 1st Corps asking them to take measures because Mr. Delalic was their subordinate. Both him and his units were subordinated to the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And one of the people who was given this was the Main Staff of the armed forces. It's on the front of the document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understood your question properly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you'd look at the front of the document. If you'd go to page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: There are people to whom it has gone. And one is Main Staff of the armed forces, the security administration, Main Staff of the armed forces, security administration. Are these -- on the right-hand side, the front of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't find it. Either I don't see it or it doesn't exist in the document that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm seeing it in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that my friend is referring to the SVB's own stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. I'll -- yes, obviously from the English version, Your Honour, there's a -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, could I just be -- it had better be cleared up from where this was sent and to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please, once again for the record, say who sent this document and who received it. I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic, the question was -- the one last question on that document: Just to make it clear and for the record who was the document sent to and who was it from? The addressor and the addressee. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The document was sent to the staff of the Supreme Command, to the administration for security, and it was sent by the under-secretary of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Jozo Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now show you another document, which is -- the 65 ter is 170. It's 04036165, and it's MFI208.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May I give the -- the Bosnian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This document is by you, isn't it, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us about this particular document. What are you doing in this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: This is the implementation of what I wrote in my own hand. One of my subordinates issued this task to the 1st Corps on my instructions, and that's why I signed this document. This was a follow-up on my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what are you asking to be done, and to who are you asking this from?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: From the security services of the 1st Corps, in paragraph 1 of this document, I am first informing them of what we had received in the previous document, describing what had happened, and I am giving them a task. This is not an order. These are tasks: To collect evidence, material, and initiate criminal procedure against the perpetrator, and inform the Supreme Command Staff security administration about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: In the document that we received from the MUP, we found the name of Mr. Ramiz Delalic. And this is the only comment I can give you, and it stems from that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you asked for investigations to be conducted and for material to be collected against Ramiz Delalic, aka Celo, by this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see this in the last paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, who was the military security officer of the 10th Brigade and under whose command was he?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The security officer of the 10th Brigade was Mr. Senad Hasic. He was subordinated to the brigade commander, Mr. Musan Topalovic, Caco. And within the scope of professional security issues, he was under the jurisdiction of the security department of the 1st Corps headed at the time by Mr. Sacir Arnautovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him for information about the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to this. Your Honours, we've now been through the witnesses from the Grabovica crime base. And the Prosecution have led and the Prosecution have culled witnesses here on the basis that they were economical with the truth and they left standing other witnesses who presumably they rely on as truthful, those including Witness D, the other Arnautovic, Erdin Arnautovic, and also a number of others, including those who were the civilians there. Now, not one of those witnesses were asked nor did they give the evidence that the 10th Brigade were present or took part in this tragedy at Grabovica. There's no evidence at all of the 10th Brigade being involved. Now, it will be apparent from the materials that the Prosecution had hopes of the 10th Brigade being established to be there, but the evidence on that score did not materialise. And in my submission, it is just irrelevant to ask questions now about the 10th Brigade. It is just irrelevant to the matters before the Court. No one is suggesting that the 10th Brigade were involved in the murders. Not one witness has. For that reason, I object to questions relating to the reputation, doings, or other performances by the 10th Brigade at any stage, frankly, because history has passed the 10th Brigade by in this trial, as far as I can adjudge the evidence. And I object therefore to that question and I indicate an objection to others to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, I think we are still in the proceedings. The Prosecution is going to present her case step by step. So at this moment, we are not sure whether the 10th Brigade is involved or not. Maybe in the future they will be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just indicate this, Your Honour, that the Prosecution really would in those circumstances have an obligation to try to elicit such evidence from the witnesses who were at the crime scene at the time. Now, we've had 9th Brigade people, and none of them were asked and indeed none of them give that evidence. I understand what Your Honour says, and, you know, the case is not over yet. But at a certain point material becomes less probative than it is prejudicial, and Your Honours have a discretion to exclude evidence like that. Now, I understand it may be that you need to hear more before you can make that decision. But again, it would be hollow for me to make the objection later when it's all in. And for that reason, I do make the objection now. I understand Your Honour's ruling of course. I'm not going to seek to traverse the ruling. But I can indicate what I indicate now, to show that I do wish to maintain this objection in relation to any such document that concerns 10th. Yes, but that's what I have to say about it at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe at this time we could ask a question to the Prosecution, whether the 10th Brigade is involved in that incident. Is that your case or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry, Your Honour. There are two levels to this. Part of the Prosecution theory is that knowing the criminality of both the 9th and 10th Brigade, they were asked to participate at the operation. So to that extent, it's relevant to the Prosecution theory that the reputation of these two brigades becomes very important for the Prosecution to establish. The criminal reputation of these two brigades. That is the basis upon which we are leading evidence in respect of both the 9th and the 10th, and that has been the position, Your Honour, in the pre-trial brief and in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you don't have the evidence to show that the 10th Brigade is involved in the tragedies in the Grabovica, that village, so what's the relevance for their, you know, so-called bad reputations before?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's very -- with respect, Your Honour, it's extremely relevant, and as Your Honour very well said, the case is built step by step. It is a step in the Prosecution case. It will come all together. And the Prosecution should not be precluded at this stage, Your Honour, from not leading evidence on what they think -- what they feel is an essential aspect of the Prosecution theory, that the -- the accused in fact asked for these brigades to participate. That is one of the Prosecution theories. And the import of this will become very obvious, Your Honour, as the case unfolds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So at this stage -- Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, you don't have an answer to your question. Does the Prosecution say that the 10th Brigade were involved in the killings or not? That ought to be answered right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution said she will lead those evidence step by step. At a later stage we'll see the whole picture of the theory of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, she does say so. That's right. But that wasn't the answer to Your Honour's question. Your Honour, the Prosecution really has an obligation to say whether or not they're proposing to lead evidence that the 10th Brigade were involved in the killings. It's a very simple question. It's not one that requires a conference. The Defence has the right to know the case we're meeting. We need to know that. And frankly the Tribunal needs to know it as well. Why can't it be answered? It's not a question of all will become clear in the future. We're now halfway through -- and although we may not be halfway through the witness numbers. We're proceeding swiftly. We've dealt with many witnesses. It's getting a bit late, Your Honour. And, to be honest, this is a simple question. It really ought to have been contained at an early stage. But anyway, now the question has been asked. I've asked it. Your Honour has asked it. And the one component that's missing is an answer. And that's what we now seek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana. Do you have answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, I don't have you know answer to that question. And with respect to this particular piece of evidence and this witness, Your Honour, I don't think it's even, I would submit, proper for a witness to be sitting and hearing all of this. Perhaps some of these issues can be brought up at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Once Your Honour has ruled that I can admit this evidence, or I can ask about it, any other question and answers, I think this should be brought up at a later stage and not with the witness in the room, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Since we still have 15 minutes to go, I will let you continue with other proceedings. Maybe we could find some other time to discuss that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will add one thing, Your Honour. Could we take 60 seconds at the end of today's proceedings to get an answer to that question? The Defence is very keen to know. Your Honour has asked it. If my friend is concerned about the witness, I will sit down and be quiet. But an answer should come today, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Jasarevic, was - and I apologise for all of this - did you ask the security officer of the 10th Brigade for any information concerning these matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There was an objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- based on an answer. My objection was raised, Your Honour, and pending an answer to that question. My friend wants to persist with it. There's an initial barrier to jump over, and that is to answer Your Honour's question. And frankly, I can't see why that can't be asked in front of the witness. That seems to me to be a -- an attempt -- well, I won't say it's an attempt to do it. It's not an attempt to do anything. But why don't we just have an answer to that question, Your Honour. And then that this is may not be objected to. It's just such an easy basic question in the case, and it really reveals a problem, in my submission, but it's -- anyway, I do object to this question because we haven't had an answer to the question I originally asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have already decided that we'll take a few minutes to discuss this issue at the end, and at this stage we'll let Ms. Chana to continue no matter what it is, the question is, to finish this part of the proceedings. You may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you must know the question by now. Can you please answer it? Did you ask any information from the military security officer of the 10th Brigade about this information?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't usual, especially for the head of the security administration, to communicate with a brigade's head of security because you have the corps level in between also. But simply because we had information that in the area of responsibility of the 10th Brigade there were certain incidents occurring, the security service of the 1st Corps failed in their communication with us to secure a normal functioning and normal reporting back to the security officer of the 10th Brigade. I used my position and authority, even my experience, to get involved on two or three occasions by getting in touch with this security officer, Mr. Senad Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what happened when you used this initiative?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The results of my conversation with Mr. Hasic, there were none to speak of. Although I tried in a number of different ways, I failed. I tried to get him in the right mood. I tried to tell him about his duties and obligations. I tried in the most humane way possible, bearing in mind the fact that he had not been trained as a security officer to, to talk him into cooperating, to talk him into treating the security organ of the 1st Corps in a fair manner. I failed, however, and I was greatly dissatisfied with this contact that I made with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what was his demeanour? What would he say to you? Did he give you a response?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember specifically. He was well behaved in a way during that conversation. But the conversation yielded no results. He refused to accept my proposals and suggestions, the purely professional ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the military security officer of the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The security officer of the 9th Brigade was Mr. Tomo Juric, an experienced security officer who had worked for the state security service in Zenica for a long time, a mature and experienced officer and someone who really knows the ins and outs of the job, unlike this person that I have just referred to, the rather young fellow, who did not have any of the professional and technical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ask him for information?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: From time to time I had more or less the same reason as with the security officer of the 10th Brigade, to get in touch with Mr. Tomo Juric. His cooperation with the security service of the 1st Corps was very good. In actual fact, Your Honours, I tried using my own position to approach those people, the brigade commanders, or anyone who was responsible in order to help in a way the security service of the 1st Corps in exercising their overall command. I tried to talk sense into them. I tried to persuade them not to commit these disciplinary errors. It was probably thanks to Mr. Tomislav Juric who very skilfully, I assume, backed me in front of Mr. Delalic that I managed to get certain results, even with Mr. Delalic. I managed to return an all-terrain vehicle that he had picked up somewhere or rather -- or rather, his people, from a French UNPROFOR unit. There was some communication. The result achieved were not those that was required, of course, but it was becoming more effective than the communication that we had with the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But what was the general relationship between the 9th, 10th Brigade, and the military security?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question really ought to be divided into two parts: What was the relationship between the 9th Brigade and the military security; and what was the relationship between the 10th Brigade and the military security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's a kind of compound question. You may break it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you take each brigade at the time. The attitude of the 9th first, and then the 10th, to the military security generally.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, based on the information that I had, the security service of the 9th Brigade and the security service of the 1st Corps had some communication. That communication probably did not yield the required results whereas the communication between the security service of the 10th Brigade and the security service of the 1st Corps was significantly poorer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know a chap called Amir Delkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move to Mr. Amir Delkic, I wonder if the time, being what it is, it might be an appropriate moment to finish the cross-examination of this witness for today and deal with the other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana, do you agree that we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was just going through my notes. Yes, perhaps this is a good, convenient point to stop, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, witness, I'm afraid that you have to stay in The Hague for another day, so you have to remember that you are still under the oath, so do not speak to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody speak to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Usher will show you out of the room. We'll see you tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana, are you ready to disclose your case to us or your theory to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I said, there are two aspects to this, Your Honour: One is the actual criminality; the other is who we have evidence of who committed the crimes. Your Honours will -- whether the -- the 10th Brigade - and now we talk about the 10th Brigade only, Your Honour - whether they actually committed any crimes on the ground in Grabovica is one issue, and the other issue is whether they had a criminal reputation and they were asked to come onto the -- onto the scene of the crime, which is they were asked to come to Grabovica. I'd like to separate these two issues. Now, in respect of the known criminal behaviour of the 10th Brigade, that is extremely relevant to show that having known the criminal reputation of this brigade, the accused nevertheless asked them to come into combat in an area and be billeted with civilians. Whether there's any evidence to show whether they in fact committed these crimes or whether members of the 10th Brigade were also part and parcel of the soldiers who committed some of the crimes, yes, we are prepared to say that as of now we do not have any evidence which we've produced to show that members of the 10th Brigade killed any one of the civilians, Croat civilians, in Grabovica. Your Honour, that is as far as I'm prepared, and if I'm allowed, to go by Your Honours in respect of answering this. So far, Your Honour, the -- the -- there is no evidence, but we also know, Your Honours, that we do not know who killed all of the civilians. We do not have all of the perpetrators' names. We have some. We do not have all of them. So the implication is still wide open as to who committed these crimes and who was brought onto the ground. Your Honour is smiling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any response from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We're grateful to the Prosecutor for clarifying the situation in the way which they have, and we'll proceed on the basis of that clarification from this point onwards in the case. And I'm very grateful to my friend for dealing with it as she has. Could I indicate therefore that my submission will be that there really is no basis for leading evidence of the criminal reputation of the 10th Brigade from now on. It's just plain irrelevant. Given what my friend says about the multiplicity of possible killers at Grabovica, one wonders what limit could ever be put. You could lead evidence that the whole Bosnian army was guilty of committing offences from time to time and that therefore they should never have been used in combat where civilians were living because there was a -- a real likelihood that they would or might commit such offences. But it's just so speculative it's not permissible for the Prosecutor to lead that evidence. To lead evidence that the 10th are devils when they have no evidence that the 10th did anything is an unsustainable proposition. The Prosecutor have clear evidence that members of the 9th Brigade committed killings. They are permitted to lead evidence concerning that reputation and to attempt to link it as best they can to the case against Mr. Halilovic and the only limit upon them there is a limit of relevance. But the 10th Brigade's reputation is now, in my submission, irrelevant and therefore no evidence should be led of it. Now, rather than deal with this as a global matter on the run, we would be prepared to -- to deal with it by way of a brief motion or we can deal with it document by document, as the Prosecution proceeds in the normal way. I don't wish to turn this into a public inquiry into the Prosecution's way of presenting the case. What I'd say though is it's quite clear now they just can't be leading evidence about the 10th when they themselves admit they have no idea whether any members of the 10th committed any murders. That's their concession, it's -- it's a realistic concession based on the evidence frankly. They've seen the evidence. It wasn't appropriate for me to raise that up until now, but now it is, and they've given it a fair answer, which we accept, so that that's the basis on which my original objection was raised and I can indicate it's going to be the basis for the future objections to the 10th Brigade material but not to the 9th Brigade material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after the consultations with my colleagues and after hearing the parties on that very issue, we believe that the principle of hearing the evidence is the relevance to this case. Any case so long as it's relevant to this case, it is admissible or usable at least in the courtroom. And now we are in the stage of the Prosecution's case and we are still in the very beginning of her case. We could not quite appreciate the whole picture of the Prosecution's case. Generally speaking the Trial Chamber could not interfere or give any instructions to either party on how to conduct their case and how to pursue their theory of the evidence in any cases. So at this stage we will allow the Prosecution to continue to present any evidence concerning of the 10th Brigade and we will see at a later stage if there's any need to alter our positions on that aspect. Of course, the Defence team has the full right to challenge the relevance of any piece of the evidence presented by the Prosecution in the future proceedings. It is so decided. So the hearing for today is adjourned, and we will meet tomorrow afternoon in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
